title: Ang 1429: the seal
hookLine: the Mundavani's plate of truth, contentment and reflection, and a closing salok of thanks
tomorrow: so what's left on the very last page?

cards: A wax seal on a letter used to say two things: it's finished, and here's whose it is. The Granth has one. It's near the end of a full reading.
The room is packed, the karah prashad sits covered by the platform, and the reader turns to ang 1429. Kids who fidgeted for an hour go still. The last hymn before the seal isn't a rule or a warning.
It's about a plate. Three things are on it, and then one more. What are they?

teach.b: Guru Arjan wrote it, and its name, Mundavani, is usually rendered as the seal.

In paraphrase: on this plate three things are placed, truth, contentment and reflection. The Name of the Lord, the nectar that holds everyone up, is placed there too. Whoever eats it, whoever savors it, is saved.
This can't be given up; keep it in your heart, always. The dark world is crossed by holding to the Lord's feet, and, Nanak, all of it is the Lord's own spread.
So the hymns of the Granth end the way a family meal ends: with a plate passed around. Not a recap of everything before it. Something to eat.
And look at what's on it. Truth, contentment, reflection: none of them can be bought, and all of them go slowly.
Then comes a salok, also Guru Arjan's, and it's pure thanks. In paraphrase: I didn't recognize what you'd done for me; you made me worthy. I had no virtue; you took pity on me yourself.
Mercy came, and I met the True Guru, my friend. Nanak says: if I receive the Name, I live, and body and mind turn green.
That's the other side of the seal. The book doesn't close on a lecture. It closes on a gift, and on gratitude for the gift.

how: When Sikhs complete a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Mundavani and the salok of thanks on ang 1429 come near the end, and the reading closes with Anand Sahib, Ardas and karah prashad shared with everyone present.

games.q: the seal on ang 1429 — tap the pairs.
p: Guru Arjan's closing hymn: the seal
the nectar placed on the plate too

s: the Granth's hymns end with a list of rules to keep
they end with a plate to eat from: truth, contentment, reflection and the Name.
after the Mundavani, Guru Arjan adds a salok of thanks
I didn't recognize what you'd done for me; you made me worthy.
the Mundavani says the plate is only for the virtuous
whoever eats it is saved, and the salok says: I had no virtue; you took pity on me.

games.q: your cousin is finishing a long school project and wants to end it by repeating every point once more. what does ang 1429 suggest about ending well?
o: set out the few things that matter, to be used, then say thank you.
go over every point again, so nothing gets lost at the very end.
add a strong warning to anyone who'd change it after you're done.
games.why: the Granth's hymns close on a plate of truth, contentment and reflection, then a salok of thanks. no recap, no warning.

practice: Read ang 1429 if it's near you. Or say the plate out loud, slowly: truth, contentment, reflection, the Name. Pause after each one, as if setting a bowl down on the table, and let the sit hold all four.
